paragraphs.heading: The most common plastic
paragraphs.text: Polyethylene, also called polythene and shortened to PE, is the plastic made in the greatest amounts. Most of it goes into packaging: plastic bags and films, geomembranes, and containers like bottles, cups and jars. As of 2017 more than 100 million tonnes of polyethylene resins were being made each year, 34% of the whole plastics market. Most kinds share the chemical formula (C₂H₄)ₙ.

paragraphs.heading: Many kinds of PE
paragraphs.text: PE is usually a mixture of similar ethylene polymers with different values of n. It comes in low-density and high-density forms and many variations, and crosslinking or copolymerization can change it further. Its properties depend strongly on molecular weight, crosslinking and the presence of comonomers. Low-density polyethylene (LDPE) is softer and more transparent than high-density polyethylene (HDPE).

paragraphs.heading: Tough and long-lived
paragraphs.text: Every form is nontoxic and chemically resilient, which helps explain its popularity. Strong acids and strong bases do not attack most grades, and the material absorbs almost no water, though non-polar gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide pass through it easily. The same resilience makes it a long-lived pollutant that resists breaking down when thrown away carelessly. Medium- and high-density grades typically melt at 120 to 130 °C, and average commercial LDPE at 105 to 115 °C.

paragraphs.heading: Two lucky accidents
paragraphs.text: The German chemist Hans von Pechmann first made polyethylene by accident in 1898 while studying diazomethane, and colleagues who examined the white, waxy product named it polymethylene. In 1933 Eric Fawcett and Reginald Gibson at Imperial Chemical Industries (ICI) in Northwich, England, stumbled on a practical route by putting ethylene and benzaldehyde under extremely high pressure. Trace oxygen in their apparatus had started the reaction, so at first it was hard to repeat. In 1935 another ICI chemist, Michael Perrin, turned it into a reliable high-pressure synthesis, the basis for industrial LDPE production from 1939.

paragraphs.heading: A wartime secret
paragraphs.text: Polyethylene has very low losses with very high frequency radio waves. So when World War II broke out, Britain stopped selling it, imposed secrecy, and used the process to make insulation for the coaxial cables of radar sets. In 1944 DuPont in Texas and Union Carbide in West Virginia began large-scale production under licence from ICI.

paragraphs.heading: Catalysts change everything
paragraphs.text: The big commercial breakthrough came with catalysts that let polymerization run at mild temperatures and pressures. The first, based on chromium trioxide, was found in 1951 by Robert Banks and J. Paul Hogan at Phillips Petroleum. In 1953 Karl Ziegler built a system from titanium halides and organoaluminium compounds that worked under even milder conditions, though the Phillips catalyst is cheaper and easier to handle, and both are heavily used. Metallocene catalysts were reported in 1976, and together with Ziegler-type catalysts they underlie today's wide range of resins, including linear low-density polyethylene.
